text.p: Copper prices veered down sharply in Firday LME trade, falling from a fresh nine month high to finish down on the day, with its weakness flowing through to other metals.
Gold prices also fell sharply on continuing worries about Swiss bank gold sales, while oil and wheat prices rose.
In Chicago, the Commodities Research Bureau index was 0.32 points higher at 245.37.

Traders said copper came under heavy pressure from liquidation and end-week sales after a midsession upside break was not sustained. Once the buying interest seen then, which was speculative in origin, faded, the market fell back swiftly.
"It has been a funny old day - and there has been no news whatsoever. The best thing you can say about copper is when it looks good you sell it, and when it looks bad you buy it," one said.
From a fresh nine-month high of $2,445 a tonne, the market tumbled back to close Friday's kerb at $2,390, a $13 loss from Thursday.
Most traders remain bullish, however, given continued stock falls - LME inventories dropped 6,225 tonnes on Friday.
Elsewhere, sentiment was pulled around by copper's volatility, with aluminium largely following the red metal.
A further heightening in the Trans-World/Russian spat over foreign involvement in Russia's domestic industry did not influence the market unduly.
After grinding to a halt near the $1,700 level the aluminiun price sagged to finish the kerb at $1,675, down $14.
Zinc came back from the fresh 4-1/2 year highs of $1,266 in late trading, but remained firmer and set for further gains.

Nickel movements were volatile throughout the session, matching the whippy copper market. Thus, prices peaked in early afternoon, before re-tracing towards the end of the session to close at $8,130, down $20 from Thursday.
Lead trading was fairly unexciting for most of the session, with the market holding in a tight, albeit steadier range. The market finished at $686, up $3.
Tin was generally supported on price dips, but was unable to make much upside progress when copper came back from its highs. Prices closed just $10 higher at $5,920.
Alloy was marked down with primary, and finished a slightly softer $1,550/55 a tonne.

CBOT soft red winter wheat futures closed higher on concerns about wet weather in some U.S. SRW wheat growing areas, another rally in soybeans and on spillover from the better-than-expected number for wheat in Thursday's USDA weekly export sales report, traders said.

The market also took note of this week's firm tone in European wheat markets, news Iraq will tender on March 11 for 50,000 tonnes of U.S. wheat. Also, traders in Manila on Friday said Philippine grain importers were expected to return to the market next week for 50,000 tonnes of whet on price dips. Wheat closed two cents per bushel higher to three lower, with March up 1-1/2 at $3.75 a bushel.
NYMEX crude ended up Friday though off its highs as a short covering rally sparked by technical strength belied ample supplies that threatened to place crude in contango.

"I think we came back since I think the screen got ahead of physical fundamentals. Refineries have to absorb a lot crude that has come in - Brent, Nigerian and everything else," said William Brown, president of trading firm W.H. Brown & Co in New York. April crude settled up 34 cents at $21.28 a barrel after rising to $21.37 earlier in the session. April heating oil ended up 0.65 cent a gallon at 54.08 cents while April gasoline finished 1.19 cents a gallon higher at 65.67 cents.

New York precious metals ended sharply lower Friday as the specter of Swiss gold sales continued to dog market sentiment, traders said. "Gold has suffered from this big dent to sentiment of having the Swiss turning on them -- it's almost like betrayal," Dinsa Mehta of Chase Manhattan said.

Bullion fell below the psychological level of $350.00 an ounce to $348.30/80 an ounce. COMEX April gold settled down $3.70 at $349.90, traded $353.50 to $349.10. Volume was estimated at 68,000 lots. Floor sources said April gold needed to stay above $349.10 to $349.40 to avoid triggering heavy sell stops.
Switzerland said earlier this week it planned to sell 40 tonnes of gold over 10 years to raise cash for victims of the Holocaust and other tragedies.
